subject: environmental-science

moments.title: Malthus's Essay on Population
moments.body: An Essay on the Principle of Population argues population tends to grow geometrically while food supply grows arithmetically, leading inevitably to checks (war, famine, disease, moral restraint). The Essay shapes Darwin's reading of competition and Victorian poor-law debates alike.
moments.takeaway: A clergyman's economic-demographic argument from 1798 reframed the relationship between population, resources and ecology for two centuries.

moments.title: The Population Bomb
moments.body: Ehrlich's bestseller predicts mass starvation in the 1970s-80s. The Green Revolution (Norman Borlaug, 1960s — Nobel Peace Prize 1970) significantly delays the predicted famines through high-yield wheat and rice. Ehrlich's specific timeline was wrong; the underlying resource concerns recurred in different forms.
moments.takeaway: Neo-Malthusian predictions of the late 1960s did not arrive on schedule. The reasons (agricultural innovation, falling birth rates) matter.

now.title: Population today
now.body: World population: ~8 billion (2022, UN estimate). Projected to peak at ~10.4 billion in 2086 then decline. Fertility is now below replacement in most of Europe, East Asia and parts of the Americas. The 21st-century challenge has flipped from population growth to population decline and ageing in many regions.
now.open_questions: Can food systems support 10 billion people sustainably? Demand-side change (diet, waste) may matter more than supply-side.

reflection: Malthus's argument is rarely correct in its details but recurs in environmental thought (Club of Rome 'Limits to Growth' 1972, planetary boundaries 2009). Whether each generation is 'Malthus was wrong' or 'Malthus was just early' depends on the time horizon.
